paper_a.title: Common Risk Factors in the Returns on Stocks and Bonds (Fama & French 1993)

paper_b.title: Arbitrage Pricing Theory (Huberman & Wang 2005, review of Ross 1976 APT)

metadata.description: Fama-French (1993) is an empirical multi-factor asset-pricing paper that proposes specific traded mimicking portfolios (RM-RF, SMB, HML, plus the bond factors TERM and DEF) and tests them via time-series regressions; Huberman-Wang (2005) is a theoretical review of the Arbitrage Pricing Theory (Ross 1976) that develops the linear factor model and exact/approximate APT pricing relation from no-arbitrage and equilibrium foundations. The two papers attack the same problem -- explaining the cross-section of expected returns by a small set of common factors -- with substantially different machinery (econometric construction and testing of mimicking portfolios vs no-arbitrage / SDF / Hilbert-space derivations of linear pricing). HW2005 explicitly cites FF1993 as a leading instance of the APT factor-specification approach. Registry expected Ross 1976 for paper_b but the actual extracted text is the 2005 Huberman-Wang review which surveys APT including Ross's contribution; the alignment therefore treats HW2005 as the theoretical-APT counterpart.

matches.explanation: FF's stated problem is to find a small set of common risk factors whose time-series regressions yield zero intercepts for every asset; HW's exact APT relation mu = i*lambda_0 + beta*lambda_1 is the theoretical statement of the same goal -- expected returns linear in factor loadings, with intercept equal to the risk-free rate. FF formulates the goal econometrically (alpha_i ~ 0 in the time-series); HW formulates it as the conclusion of a no-arbitrage argument. Same conceptual target, different framing.

FF's three-factor stock regression R_i - RF = a + b*(RM-RF) + s*SMB + h*HML + e is a concrete instance of HW's general factor model r = mu + beta*f + e (and the time-series form r_t = alpha + beta*f_t + e_t). The factor loadings (b, s, h) play the role of beta; the residual e_i is the idiosyncratic noise. Match is exact up to (i) FF specifying particular traded factors (RM-RF, SMB, HML) and (ii) FF expressing the regression in excess-return form. Confidence high despite PDF-fallback because the algebraic structures align line by line.

FF's five-factor regression and bond two-factor regression are further instances of HW's general factor model with k=5 and k=2 respectively. Same correspondence as EP371.2 <-> DP372.1 but with different factor-set specifications; bundled here so the FF nodes are not repeatedly mapped to the same generic model.

FF's TP371.1 cites the Merton (1973) ICAPM and Ross (1976) APT result that, when the explanatory returns are good mimicking portfolios, the time-series intercepts are zero. HW's DP372.3 / EP372.3 state the exact APT relation mu = i*lambda_0 + beta*lambda_1 (zero intercepts after subtracting the risk-free rate); TP372.6 is the iff characterization (exact APT holds iff E[eM]=0). FF cites this as external prior work; HW develops it as the central theoretical object. Same theorem stated from the empiricist's and theorist's sides.

FF's RM-RF (excess market return), SMB (Small Minus Big), and HML (High Minus Low) factor portfolios are precisely the objects HW describes in ExP372.1 (`Fama-French Three-Factor Application`): `the equity-market return, the small-minus-big size spread, and the value-minus-growth (book-to-market) spread`. HW cites Fama-French 1993 by name. This is a paper-origin (FF) <-> external-origin (HW citing FF) match -- strong signal that HW reads FF as a leading APT factor specification.

FF's GRS F-test (statistic EP371.6, theorem TP371.3 from Gibbons-Ross-Shanken 1989, application ClP371.6 rejecting at the 0.95 level) and HW's likelihood-ratio statistic LR = T(log|barOmega| - log|hatOmega|) ~ chi^2_{n-k-1} (within AP372.1) are both finite-sample joint tests of the null that all pricing intercepts are zero under the candidate factor model. Same null hypothesis, different test statistics (F vs chi^2) arising from different distributional setups; analogous rather than exact.

Both are equilibrium asset-pricing statements: FF's TP371.2 is the Sharpe-Lintner CAPM (one-factor pricing with market beta and zero intercept); HW's TP372.7 is Connor's (1984) k+1 fund separation in which every investor holds a well-diversified portfolio and exact APT obtains in competitive equilibrium. CAPM is the k=1 special case of factor-equilibrium pricing; Connor generalises it to k factors. Both are cited as external in their host papers.

Composite many-to-many (parent-skipped per v2 rule): HW's two-step empirical APT test (AP372.1) is the general estimation recipe -- estimate the unrestricted factor model (EP372.8 OLS estimators), then the restricted-by-exact-APT model (EP372.9 / EP372.10), then compute the LR. FF instantiates the unrestricted side by specifying particular factors and running the time-series regressions EP371.2 / EP371.3. The restricted-side / LR portion of HW's algorithm corresponds to FF's GRS test (covered separately). The L2 algorithm_step children of AP372.1 (ASP372.1-3) are subsumed implicitly under this parent-skipped composite.

Excess return R_i - RF is a primitive used in FF's regressions. HW writes returns as r without explicit excess-return centering (the risk-free rate appears as lambda_0 in the pricing equation). Conceptually trivial, but HW has no node defining `excess return` per se.
Book-to-market equity (BE/ME) is a firm-level accounting/market measure used by FF to sort stocks. HW references the BE/ME spread only via the FF citation in ExP372.1; no theoretical counterpart.
Size (ME) is a firm-level market measure used by FF. HW references the size spread only via the FF citation in ExP372.1; no theoretical counterpart.

FF's six size-BE/ME building-block portfolios are a concrete econometric construction used to form SMB and HML. HW does not specify portfolio-construction recipes; portfolio formation is outside its scope.

TERM (long-term government bond return minus T-bill rate) is a specific empirical proxy for unexpected interest-rate shifts. HW gives no analogous concrete factor; the closest neighbour is HW's external ExP372.3 (Chen-Roll-Ross macro factors).

DEF (corporate minus government bond return) is a specific empirical proxy for default risk. As with TERM, HW reviews factor specification only abstractly (RP372.1) and has no matching concrete factor.
FF's 25 size-BE/ME test portfolios are the empirical assets used as dependent variables. HW makes no analogous portfolio specification.
Bond test portfolios (government maturity groups + Moody's rating groups) have no counterpart in HW's purely theoretical review.

RMO (orthogonalized market factor) is a regression-residual construct FF use to decompose RM-RF into a part orthogonal to SMB, HML, TERM, DEF. Pure econometric tool with no counterpart in HW's theoretical APT.
FF's empirical decomposition regression of RM-RF on SMB, HML, TERM, DEF (with the reported coefficients and R^2=0.38) is a paper-specific empirical finding. HW has no such empirical decomposition.

FF's residual-predictability test regression (residuals on D/P, DFS, TS, RF) is a robustness diagnostic. HW reviews APT estimation/testing in general (AP372.1, AP372.2) but not this particular residual-predictability check.

FF's main empirical claim -- that three stock factors plus two bond factors capture common variation and average returns for 32 test portfolios -- is the central FF contribution. HW does not endorse or refute any specific factor set; it surveys the theoretical apparatus and explicitly notes (RP372.1, RP372.2) that factor specification is a separate empirical question.

FF's claim that intercepts in the three-factor regression are close to zero across the 25 size-BE/ME portfolios is the empirical analogue of HW's exact APT relation mu = i*lambda_0 + beta*lambda_1. The match is `analogous` (not `exact`) because FF's claim is a finite-sample empirical statement (only 2 of 25 intercepts exceed 0.2%/month) while HW's is the exact-pricing identity from no-arbitrage. Same target, different epistemic status.
FF empirical claim that TERM and DEF capture common variation in bonds is paper-specific and has no analogue in HW's theoretical review.
FF empirical claim that TERM and DEF also capture common variation in stocks is paper-specific.
FF empirical claim that five-factor regressions reveal term-structure factors in stocks (using RMO) is paper-specific.
FF's robustness claim that five-factor residuals are not predictable by D/P, DFS, TS, RF is paper-specific.
FF's January-seasonals robustness claim is paper-specific.
FF's split-sample validation claim is paper-specific.
FF's claim that the three-factor model also explains E/P and D/P portfolios is a paper-specific out-of-sample empirical finding.
FF's open problem (what fundamentals drive size and BE/ME factors) is a forward-looking empirical question. HW does not pose this question.

HW's approximate APT inequality (mu - X*lambda)' Z^-1 (mu - X*lambda) <= a is a theoretical bound on mean-squared pricing error. FF works only with finite-sample point estimates of intercepts; no analogous theoretical bound.

Well-diversified portfolio (idiosyncratic variance to zero in the limit) is a theoretical asymptotic object central to HW's no-arbitrage derivation. FF's portfolios are well-diversified in practice but FF does not invoke the formal definition.

HW's SDF-derived pricing decomposition mu = i*lambda_0 + beta*lambda_1 + alpha is the theoretical bridge from utility maximization to APT. FF takes the multifactor implication as given (TP371.1) and does not derive it from an SDF.

HW's cross-sectional regression equation (Fama-MacBeth-style: hat_mu on (i, hat_beta), optionally augmented by characteristics z) is a methodological cousin of FF's time-series regressions but is itself an external citation in HW (Black-Jensen-Scholes 1972, Fama-MacBeth 1973). FF1993 uses time-series, not cross-sectional Fama-MacBeth, regressions, so genuinely absent on the FF side.

HW's investor utility-maximization problem (deriving the SDF from first-order conditions) is the equilibrium foundation FF takes as given. FF poses an econometric problem (ProbP371.1), not a utility-maximization problem.
HW's exact-APT-for-well-diversified-portfolios theorem (iff in the limit) is theoretical with no FF counterpart.
Proof sketch of Huberman's APT bound (orthogonal projection + arbitrage construction). FF presents no proofs of analogous theoretical statements.
Proof for well-diversified portfolios (rescaling argument). FF has no analogous proof.
Proof sketch of Ingersoll's generalisation (non-diagonal Z via U U^T factorisation). FF has no analogous proof.
HW proposition deriving the APT bound from the SDF first-order condition (utility-based). FF has no analogous derivation.
